page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: The comparison itself / the ranking rationale - 'For a second option, and the drug to beat: plain lidocaine, already in the syringe'
sentence_as_it_stands: It has by far the largest body of evidence behind it, the least painful injection of any solution measured, and the only sting that can be taken all the way to body pH by buffering.
quote: The effect of the buffering of the lo … cal anesthetic solutions was a raising … of the pH toward a more physiologic … range of 7.0 to 7.4 (Table 1). … The amount of pain associated with … the infiltration of the local anesthetic … solutions was dramatically reduced by … buffering (Figure).
corrected_wording: It has by far the largest body of evidence behind it and the least painful injection of any solution measured. It is not the only one of these drugs whose solution has been brought into the physiological pH range and measured there: a randomised, prospective, double-blind, within-subject study of 25 volunteers injected buffered and unbuffered mepivacaine intradermally alongside the two lidocaine solutions, reported every buffered solution inside 7.0 to 7.4, and found the pain of infiltration far lower for the buffered member of all three pairs, with the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick not significantly different between the members of the mepivacaine pair (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545). The laboratory study already cited in this record on the bupivacaine page reports the same for mepivacaine on a precipitation endpoint (AlShammari 2025).
notes: This is a uniqueness statement inside the sentence that ranks plain lidocaine as the drug to beat, so part of the ordering rests on it. The paper's own three unbuffered solutions and three buffered solutions are reported with their measured pH in its Table 1, and the buffered mepivacaine sits in the physiological range alongside the buffered lidocaine solutions. Written here as what the study did and found, with nothing about how any solution was made: no agent, no ratio, no volumes. Two caveats worth keeping. First, this paper rated pain on a 0-to-10 scale, not the 100 mm scale the page's table uses, so the numbers do not belong on that table's scale. Second, within this paper the buffered mepivacaine pair scored numerically lower than the buffered lidocaine pair, but the three drugs were never compared against one another by any test, so that is not a measured reversal of 'the least painful injection of any solution measured' and is not claimed as one here.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each one cost in injection pain? (the table and its opening sentence)
sentence_as_it_stands: The available figures come from three different settings and do not belong on one scale, so the table says which is which.
quote: Each participant then was asked to in … dicate on the Visual Analogue Scale … the number that corresponded to his … or her perception of the amount of … pain associated with the infiltration of … the anesthetic solution. The Visual
corrected_wording: The available figures come from four different settings and do not belong on one scale, so the table says which is which. The fourth is intradermal, in 25 volunteers who each received all six solutions at six sites: plain and buffered lidocaine, plain and buffered lidocaine with epinephrine, and plain and buffered mepivacaine, each rated on a 0-to-10 scale (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545). It carries an intradermal figure for plain mepivacaine's injection pain, which the table does not.
notes: The table's rows cover lidocaine with epinephrine and bupivacaine with epinephrine in digital blocks, three plain drugs at matched pH intradermally, ropivacaine intradermally, mepivacaine with epinephrine in digital blocks, and plain bupivacaine. Plain mepivacaine and plain lidocaine have no intradermal row, and this paper measured both, in the same subjects, by Visual Analogue Scale, in a randomised double-blind design. Its scale is 0 to 10 rather than 100 mm, so the figures cannot be dropped into the existing table without saying so, which is why the correction adds a setting rather than a number. The elements that sit on the page's own injection-pain table, and the pH-matched row in particular, are not disturbed: this study matched no pH between drugs and never compared the three against one another.

section: Sources — How long the numbness lasts (Collins 2013 annotation); and the body passage 'One study points at a longer figure'
sentence_as_it_stands: The only human study using the correct depth, intradermal, with [dose figure omitted] lidocaine and [dose figure omitted]: duration 6 h 38 min to 7 h 25 min across four mixtures in 25 volunteers.
quote: three local anesthetics ([dose figure omitted] lidocaine, [dose figure omitted] lidocaine with [dose figure omitted] epi … nephrine, and [dose figure omitted] mepivacaine) were investigated in a randomized, prospec … tive, double-blind study of 25 adult volunteers. … of the three local anesthetics were prepared, and a [dose figure omitted] intradermal injection … of each was administered.
corrected_wording: The only human study that times the duration of that mixture at the correct depth, intradermal: duration 6 h 38 min to 7 h 25 min across four mixtures in 25 volunteers. It is not the only human intradermal study of the mixture. Christoph 1988 (PMID 2827545) injected it intradermally in a randomised, prospective, double-blind, within-subject study of 25 volunteers, and recorded onset and the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick rather than a duration, stopping measurement in the first few minutes.
notes: This settles claim C081, which the abstract left uncertain. The paper names the mixture at exactly the strengths the annotation names, in its title sentence, in its methods list of solutions and in its table of measured solution pH, and injects it intradermally through a 25-gauge needle by a blinded investigator. So the uniqueness as written does not hold; narrowed to timing the duration, it does. Nothing here touches Collins's duration figures, which remain the only intradermal timings of the mixture, nor the page's separate point that the Collins endpoint is return of pinprick sensation in healthy forearm skin. The body passage's clause 'unlike every other study in this section' stays true of the studies that section cites, since this paper is cited nowhere on the page.

section: The recommendation ('Mepivacaine is not the longer wheal it looks like'); and 'How long does a mepivacaine block actually last? > In skin, which is the tissue that matters here'
sentence_as_it_stands: The only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981).
quote: the diameter of the area of the … skin anesthetized to pinprick was … identified and marked on the tape. … Measures of skin anesthe … sia were carried out for 4V2 minutes.
corrected_wording: The study that mapped it across concentrations in human skin, by the test you would use — pinprick over an intradermal bleb — found recovery complete or nearly complete within 2 hours at every concentration tested, with time to half-recovery levelling off between about 40 and 70 minutes (Fairley and Reynolds, 1981). It is not the only study to have pricked the skin over a mepivacaine bleb: this page's own second source timed recovery the same way (Willatts and Reynolds, 1985), and a randomised double-blind study of 25 volunteers marked the area of skin anaesthetised to pinprick around an intradermal mepivacaine wheal, though only across the first few minutes, so it yields no duration (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545).
notes: Two separate points, one of which answers the question put to this paper. First, 'the only study that measured it in human skin, by the test you would use' is broader than the duration point it supports, and the page itself says two paragraphs later that two studies have measured this; a third study pricked the skin over a mepivacaine wheal without timing it. Second, and this is what the paper settles: W-M001 says the only study measuring mepivacaine in human skin by pinprick over an intradermal bleb is Fairley and Reynolds 1981, and this paper did measure mepivacaine in human skin by pinprick over an intradermal wheal, but it did not measure duration. It recorded the area insensitive to pinprick at six readings inside the first 4 1/2 minutes and then stopped, with that area still rising at the last reading, so it adds a human intradermal pinprick measurement of mepivacaine and no duration figure at all. Its abstract's phrase 'duration of skin anesthesia' is therefore not a measurement it made, which is worth recording so the abstract is not read as a third skin duration. How many studies have timed mepivacaine in skin is settled from Reynolds 1976, not from here.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: Sources › What has no source — 'The 2.5-hour duration for mepivacaine'
sentence_as_it_stands: The 2.5-hour duration for mepivacaine. It circulates widely and comes from dental work. No source for it in skin was found, and the two studies that did time mepivacaine in skin both came in far below it.
quote: Measures of skin anesthe … sia were carried out for 4V2 minutes.
corrected_wording: The 2.5-hour duration for mepivacaine. It circulates widely and comes from dental work. No source for it in skin was found. One study that looks like a source is not one: a randomised double-blind intradermal study of mepivacaine in 25 volunteers reports in its abstract that duration of skin anaesthesia was unaltered by buffering, but its skin measurement ran only across the first few minutes and recorded the area numbed rather than a duration, and its statement about duration is carried over from nerve-block and epidural work and from the authors' own uncontrolled clinical impression (Christoph 1988, PMID 2827545).
notes: The first half of the sentence is confirmed from this paper's full text: it is not a source for 2.5 hours in skin. Recorded as now-verified because the sentence is right on that half and because the full text closes off a candidate a reader would otherwise reach for, this paper being indexed under mepivacaine administration and dosage with 'duration of skin anesthesia' in its abstract. The count in the second half ('the two studies') is not settled from here and is addressed from Reynolds 1976; nothing in this finding endorses it.
